title: Custom Properties and Reusable Values
summary: Define reusable design values for color, spacing, and other repeated decisions.

sketchBlocks.title: Store repeated decisions in :root

tryItExercises.title: Centralize repeated design decisions
tryItExercises.prompt:
## CSS task

The site is responsive now, but its accent colors and spacing are still written as separate literal values. That makes future polish harder because the same design decision has to be remembered in several places. Custom properties give those repeated choices names without changing the page yet. In `styles.css`, add a `:root` rule defining `--color-accent: #1d4ed8`, `--color-accent-strong: #1e40af`, and `--space-section: 1.5rem`. The preview should look the same after this step—that is intentional; you are building the shared design controls that the next changes will use.

### File to edit

`styles.css`

### Check your work

Keep the site's existing cumulative work, make the requested change, then compare the **Preview** with the **Expected result** before moving on.
tryItExercises.hint: Define the three custom properties in `:root`; this step prepares reusable values, so no visible change is expected yet.

help.concept: Custom properties centralize repeated design decisions before those values are consumed by visible rules.
help.hint_1: Place the three `--name: value;` declarations inside one `:root` rule.
help.hint_2: Do not replace existing styles yet; the next exercises will consume these values.

sketchBlocks.title: Consume values with var()

tryItExercises.title: Use the shared accent across links
tryItExercises.prompt:
## CSS task

The portfolio already uses accent colors, but the links do not yet share the new design token. Instead of hard-coding another `color`, make the reusable value control them. Add an `a` rule with `color: var(--color-accent);`. Check several pages in the preview: ordinary links should now use the same blue accent, and changing the token later would update them from one place.

### File to edit

`styles.css`

### Check your work

Keep the site's existing cumulative work, make the requested change, then compare the **Preview** with the **Expected result** before moving on.
tryItExercises.hint: Use `var(--color-accent)` in an `a` rule so the shared token, not another literal `color`, controls link text.

help.concept: Consuming a custom property turns a named design decision into a visible reusable style.
help.hint_1: Use the `var()` function inside the link `color` declaration.
help.hint_2: Keep the existing stylesheet intact and add the new link rule cumulatively.

sketchBlocks.title: Reuse one value in layout

tryItExercises.title: Give the layout more breathing room with one spacing token
tryItExercises.prompt:
## CSS task

The responsive Grid works, but its content still feels tighter than the rest of the polished layout. You already created a shared section-spacing value, so reuse it instead of introducing another number. Set `main`'s `gap` to `var(--space-section)`. Compare the preview before and after: the content blocks should feel a little less crowded while the responsive Grid behavior stays the same.

### File to edit

`styles.css`

### Check your work

Keep the site's existing cumulative work, make the requested change, then compare the **Preview** with the **Expected result** before moving on.
tryItExercises.hint: Reuse `--space-section` for `main`'s `gap` so the spacing comes from the shared design system.

help.concept: A spacing token keeps repeated layout rhythm consistent and easy to adjust.
help.hint_1: Add a later `main` rule that sets `gap` with `var(--space-section)`.
help.hint_2: Watch the distance between Grid items in the preview rather than changing the HTML.

quizDraft.title: Choose the reusable value
quizDraft.prompt: Which CSS feature stores a reusable value such as a color or spacing decision?
quizDraft.hint: Compare each option by the role it plays in a reusable CSS design system. Use the prompt to decide which behaviors actually fit.

help.concept: Reusable CSS values centralize design decisions so the stylesheet can apply the same intent consistently in multiple places.
help.hint_1: Judge each option by its CSS behavior rather than by familiar terminology.
help.hint_2: Eliminate choices that introduce unrelated layout, markup, or duplicated design decisions.

quizDraft.title: Build a custom-property rule
quizDraft.prompt: Put the pieces in order to define and then consume an accent color.
quizDraft.hint: Start with the variable declaration, close that rule, then use var() in the element rule.

help.concept: The custom property must be declared before the later rule consumes it.
help.hint_1: Start with the variable declaration, close that rule, then use var() in the element rule.
help.hint_2: Keep the cumulative site intact and make only the focused change required by this exercise.

quizDraft.title: Consume a custom property
quizDraft.hint: The blank is the retrieval part of the declaration. Compare the choices by which one reads a named custom property.

help.concept: A declared custom property is useful only when another declaration retrieves its stored value.
help.hint_1: Look for the CSS choice whose job is to retrieve a named custom property's value.
help.hint_2: The completed color declaration should read the existing design token without redefining it.

quizDraft.title: Name a custom property
quizDraft.hint: The blank is the reusable name being declared inside the shared scope. Choose the option that follows CSS custom-property naming syntax.

help.concept: Custom-property names use a distinctive CSS naming pattern so they can be declared once and referenced later.
help.hint_1: Compare the choices by which one has the required custom-property naming form.
help.hint_2: The completed declaration should create the shared spacing token used later in the layout.
